subject: House hacking: live (almost) for free in a 2-4 unit
preheader: 3.5% down FHA · The year-2 transition where break-even flips to real cash flow · True out-of-pocket math

marketSnapshot.headline: House hacking — the highest-leverage path into rental investing
marketSnapshot.body: House hacking means buying a 2-4 unit property with owner-occupant financing (FHA 3.5%, conventional 5%), living in one unit, and renting the others. After year 1 you can move out and the property converts to a pure investment. The leverage advantage is enormous — you control a $300-400k property with $10-20k down instead of $75-100k for a pure investment. The year-2 math is where the strategy really compounds.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: True out-of-pocket: $0 · all units cover your costs
dealSpotter.body: A $300k triplex with two units renting at $1,400 each = $2,800/mo of incoming rent. Total monthly cost of property (mortgage + tax + insurance + utilities for your unit + reserves) ~$2,750/mo. True out-of-pocket: roughly zero. You live in unit 1 for free while building equity in property you own. Exceptional and rare — finding deals like this requires hunting in undersupplied 2-4 unit markets like Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Indianapolis, parts of the Midwest.

A $400k duplex in a livable city neighborhood. Other unit rents for $1,800; you live in the equivalent unit. True out-of-pocket housing cost ~$500/mo when comparable 2-bedroom rents go for $1,500-1,900 in the area. Paying a fraction of market rent for your unit AND building principal each month. Year-2 transition: you move out, rent your unit for $1,800. Property now has $3,600/mo gross — solid cash flow.

dealSpotter.address: Example: house hack that doesn't pencil
dealSpotter.headlineNumber: True out-of-pocket: $1,600/mo · close to market rent
dealSpotter.body: A $550k 2-unit in an expensive market. Other unit rents for $2,200. True out-of-pocket $1,650/mo — close to what a comparable 1-bed rents for in the area. You're not getting meaningful housing-cost reduction AND you're carrying the operational complexity of being a landlord while living in the building. Skip — buy a regular primary residence or wait for a different deal.

blogFeature.title: House hacking explained: how to (almost) live for free in a 2-4 unit
blogFeature.excerpt: Full math behind FHA 3.5% vs conventional 5% owner-occupant loans, the year-2 transition where break-even flips to real cash flow, and the property characteristics that make a 2-4 unit work for this strategy.

qa.question: FHA 3.5% down or conventional 5% down for the house hack?
qa.answer: Conventional 5% usually wins long-term, FHA 3.5% wins short-term. FHA's lower down payment is offset by MIP (Mortgage Insurance Premium) that lasts the LIFE of the loan (or 11 years if you put 10%+ down) at typically 0.55-0.85% of the loan annually. On a $300k loan that's $1,650-2,550/year of MIP recurring forever. Conventional 5% owner-occupant loans (Fannie Mae HomeReady, Freddie Mac Home Possible) have PMI that falls off automatically at 80% LTV — typically 5-7 years in. Run both scenarios through a calculator (TrueCap supports both) and you'll usually see conventional 5% has better long-term economics IF you can come up with the extra $4-5k of down payment. FHA wins when capital is genuinely the constraint or your DTI is tight.
